candidate.title: PyPI trusted-publishing upload is gated only by writer-editable workflow logic; whether a non-release writer can publish depends on unobserved `pypi` environment and tag protections
candidate.description: publish.yml uploads to PyPI with OIDC trusted publishing whenever a GitHub release is published (publish.yml:13-16, 86-92, 130-131). The only source-visible gate is check_release_tag.py, which compares the tag string with the pyproject version. Nothing binds the tagged commit to main, even though release.md says releases are cut from main. Suppose a principal has write access but no release authority, such as a collaborator, a bot, or a compromised writer token. They could push a branch carrying modified code with the matching version line, publish a release on a tag pointing at it, and the workflow would build and upload that code as vfs-py. They could also edit publish.yml on a branch to drop the `if: github.event_name == 'release'` guard and dispatch it. The workflow file comes from the triggering ref, so neither in-source gate stops a writer. The hosted controls decide the outcome: protection rules on the `pypi` environment (required reviewers, deployment branch and tag policy), tag rulesets for v*, the collaborator list, and the PyPI trusted-publisher binding. None is observable in source. Fork contributors cannot reach this path, because release and dispatch both require write access.
candidate.claimed_root_cause: The release source identity (tagged commit and triggering ref) is never bound to reviewed main inside the workflow. The `pypi` environment is the only control that could bind it, and its configuration is not in source.

candidate.title: Glob patterns compile to backtracking regex with unbounded wildcards, so one call can stall the shared event loop
candidate.description: A caller who can run glob (or grep/glean with globs) supplies a short pattern with k wildcards. Matching it against each stored name or path of length n costs O(n^k) in CPython re. The match runs synchronously on the event loop for every candidate row, before visibility filtering. A '[...]' class disables the SQL prefilter, so every row in the mount is a candidate.
candidate.root_cause: _translate emits backtracking [^/]* and (?:.+/)? for wildcards with no cap on wildcard count or pattern length. compile_glob uses Python re, not the linear-time Rust engine. The match runs inline on the loop with no deadline.
candidate.intended_behavior: Glob matching is linear in subject length, like the Rust regex engine that grep already uses, or it is bounded by a wildcard cap and a deadline, and it never blocks other callers on the shared loop.

Each '*' becomes a backtracking [^/]*, compiled with Python re at line 208.

candidate.title: grant() is checked only at the addressed path, so a caller with read_write from the everyone posture can grant itself (or anyone) read_write over a private posture hole beneath
candidate.description: Before a grant or revoke, the grant verbs check one thing: does the caller hold read_write at the exact path it addressed? That check counts read_write the caller gets from the everyone level (the posture). The row a grant writes, though, covers the path and its whole subtree. Grant rows only ever add access, and a principal's grant outranks any deeper, narrower posture. Take a mount whose ancestor posture gives everyone read_write (the default for a fresh mount) and whose child folder has a narrower posture, such as none: the documented 'open root with a private child' shape. On that mount, any named principal can grant itself read_write at the ancestor and then read, overwrite, and re-posture the private child. So can anonymous through the router, by granting to a principal it names. The caller held nothing in that child. delete/move/sweep run a subtree check that catches this very posture hole. grant and revoke do not.
candidate.root_cause: _grant_refusal (rights.py:1305-1336) reads only the posture rows on the addressed path's ancestor chain (ancestors_and_self, line 1327). It passes as soon as Rights.reaches(path, label) is true (line 1332). reaches (grants.py:477-479) is a point test: everyone_level >= need at the path itself, or the caller's spans cover that one path. It never asks whether the caller holds the level across the subtree the new row will cover. grant_rows then upserts a principal row at path (rights.py:919, 1356-1376). resolve and Rights.covers/admits (grants.py:150-152, 485-494, 624-629) apply that row to every path beneath, even under posture holes, because principal rows only widen.
candidate.intended_behavior: Spec 058 (line 74): the granting subject set must hold read_write on the path, 'and may grant at most its own level (attenuation)'. The router docstring (base.py:1614-1615) says 'so nobody grants more than it holds'. The grant_rows docstring (rights.py:909-910) says 'what it grants never exceeds its own level there'. Spec 058 (line 64) requires subtree mutations to check beneath the target 'since an owner-floor row or a posture hole can sit inside a writable directory'. A grant or revoke at /P should be refused unless the granter holds read_write throughout /P's subtree, either by its own covering spans or with no posture row beneath /P giving everyone less than read_write.

remediation.strategy: Make the grant and revoke gate check the subtree the row will cover, not just the addressed point. When the caller's own spans do not cover the whole subtree at read_write (rights.whole or rights.covers_subtree(path)), read the posture ('*') rows strictly beneath path. candidate.description: The reindex embed step always restarts at chunk id 0. A batch the provider refuses deterministically has no split, skip or per-row quarantine. Its rows stay NULL and form the same first batch on every later run. A principal with write access to any path on the mount can write about 4096 small CJK files (about 2 MB). After that, every chunk any principal writes later never gets a vector, across any number of reindex runs, and glean's vector leg misses all of it. A smaller amount of such text permanently leaves the neighbouring rows that share its batch (other principals' content) unembedded, and slows the rest to one page per run.

A refused batch without Retry-After should be bisected down to single rows, and a single row still refused should be quarantined with a per-row failed state that select_unembedded skips and the report counts.
